title: Joseph Hated, Stripped, and Sold
summary: Jacob’s favouritism and Joseph’s dreams inflame his brothers’ hatred until they strip him, sell him to traders bound for Egypt, and deceive their grieving father.
historicalContext: Jacob has returned from Haran, buried Rachel near Bethlehem, and settled with his flocks in the vale of Hebron (35:16-27). Joseph is seventeen, which by the ages given in Genesis places Jacob near 108 and means Isaac, whose death was recorded in advance to close his story (35:29), was in fact still living. The family are semi-nomadic herdsmen who also sow grain, driving their flocks north to the well-watered pastures around Shechem, where Jacob owned land (33:19) and where his sons had recently massacred the town (chapter 34). Dothan lay on the trunk road that carried caravans from Gilead and Damascus down the coast to Egypt. Spice traders, dry rock-cut cisterns, a slave price of twenty shekels, and an Egyptian name like Potiphar all fit the world of the early second millennium BC, when Egyptian records list many Asiatic household slaves.
literaryContext: With the heading “These are the generations of Jacob” (37:2) Genesis opens its tenth and final section, which runs to the burial of Joseph in 50:26. The focus moves from Jacob to his sons, chiefly Joseph and Judah. Chapter 37 has two movements: Joseph is set apart by a father’s love, a princely robe, and two dreams (vv. 1-11); then he is sent, seized, stripped, and sold, and the robe returns to Jacob soaked in goat’s blood (vv. 12-36). The robe binds the chapter together and Joseph’s story will keep turning on garments (39:12; 41:14, 42). Old patterns resurface: a favoured son, brothers’ hatred, a kid of the goats used to deceive a father. God is not named once, yet the anonymous man at Shechem, the passing caravan, and Joseph’s arrival in an Egyptian household show his hand at work. Chapter 38 then turns aside to Judah before the story resumes in 39:1.
themes: The rejected brother destined to rule

outline.title: The Favoured Son and the Princely Robe
outline.summary: Jacob settles in Canaan, Joseph reports his brothers’ evil, and Jacob’s open favouritism, sealed by a special robe, turns the brothers’ resentment into hatred.

outline.title: Two Dreams of Bowing
outline.summary: Joseph tells of sheaves and then of sun, moon, and stars bowing to him; his brothers hate and envy him, while Jacob rebukes him yet keeps the matter in mind.

outline.title: Sent to Seek His Brothers
outline.summary: Jacob sends Joseph from Hebron to check on his brothers, and a stranger near Shechem directs him on to Dothan.

outline.title: The Plot, the Pit, and the Price
outline.summary: The brothers plan murder; Reuben steers them to a dry pit, and Judah proposes selling Joseph to a passing caravan for twenty pieces of silver.

outline.title: A Bloodied Robe and a Father’s Grief
outline.summary: Reuben finds the pit empty, the brothers deceive Jacob with the blood-dipped robe, Jacob mourns inconsolably, and Joseph is sold to Potiphar in Egypt.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger, in the land of Canaan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger.” After the long register of Esau’s descendants and the kings who reigned in Edom (chapter 36), the narrative returns to the line that carries the promise. Esau had moved away to Mount Seir because the land could not hold both brothers and their herds (36:6-8). Jacob stays in Canaan, the land God had sworn to Abraham and Isaac and had confirmed to Jacob himself at Bethel (35:12).

The wording sets two verbs side by side. Jacob “dwelt” or settled, while Isaac had lived there as a “stranger,” a resident alien without title to the soil. The phrase “the land of his father’s sojournings” recalls that the patriarchs owned no more of Canaan than a burial cave and a field near Shechem (23:17-20; 33:19). Hebrews describes them as foreigners in the land of promise who lived in tents and looked for a city with foundations (Hebrews 11:9-10). Jacob’s settling in is therefore no claim of possession; it is faith staying put where God has placed it.

The verse also stands as a quiet contrast with Edom. Esau’s line has already produced chiefs and kings (36:31), while Jacob’s family is still a household of shepherds. God’s purpose often moves more slowly through the chosen line, and the story that follows will show how much refining that household needed before it could become a nation.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּשֶׁב (vayyeshev) — and dwelt
wordNotes.explanation: From yashav, “to sit, remain, settle.” It describes taking up residence and is used of Lot settling in the cities of the plain (Genesis 13:12) and of Esau settling in Seir (Genesis 36:8). Here it marks Jacob remaining in Canaan, the place of promise, while his brother lives elsewhere.

wordNotes.term: מְגוּרֵי אָבִיו (megure aviv) — wherein his father was a stranger
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the sojournings of his father.” The noun comes from gur, “to dwell as an alien,” a person living among others without the rights of a native. God called Canaan “the land wherein thou art a stranger” when he promised it to Abraham’s seed (Genesis 17:8), and Jacob used the same language of his own life as a pilgrimage before Pharaoh (Genesis 47:9).

verses.bibleText: These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren; and the lad was with the sons of Bilhah, and with the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives: and Joseph brought unto his father their evil report.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These are the generations of Jacob.” This is the last of the ten headings that structure Genesis (2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 11:27; 25:19; and others), and it introduces the account of what came from Jacob, that is, the history of his family. The heading names Jacob, yet the very next word is “Joseph.” From here to the end of the book Jacob is still present and honoured, but the action belongs chiefly to his sons, above all to Joseph and Judah. Jacob’s seventeen years with Joseph at the start of the story will be matched by Joseph’s care for his father during Jacob’s last seventeen years in Egypt (47:28).

Joseph is “seventeen years old” and is “feeding the flock with his brethren.” The Hebrew can also be read as “shepherding his brothers among the flock,” and some have seen a hint of the leadership to come, though the plain sense is that he worked with them. The narrator adds that “the lad was with the sons of Bilhah, and with the sons of Zilpah”: Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. The term “lad” here likely signals that he served as their helper or junior. Bilhah had been Rachel’s maid, and after Rachel’s death the young Joseph may well have stayed closest to her household.

“And Joseph brought unto his father their evil report.” The word for report usually describes damaging talk, sometimes slander (Numbers 14:36-37; Proverbs 10:18). The text leaves unclear whether Joseph saw the misconduct himself or passed on what others said about it, and it does not say what the brothers had done. Given Simeon and Levi’s violence at Shechem (34:25-31) and Reuben’s sin with Bilhah (35:22), there is little reason to doubt that real wrongdoing lay behind the report. Joseph’s loyalty to his father and his unwillingness to share in evil are commendable.

Yet the narrator does not portray Joseph as a polished saint at this stage. A younger brother who carries reports to the father, and who will soon parade his dreams, was bound to be resented. Scripture values both faithfulness and wisdom in speech (Proverbs 11:13; 17:9). The Joseph of Genesis 37 is a young man of sound principle whose character has yet to be tempered by suffering. God would use slavery, false accusation, and prison to shape the seventeen-year-old who carried tales into the thirty-year-old who could rule with discretion (41:46).

wordNotes.term: אֵלֶּה תֹּלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב (elleh toledot ya‘aqov) — these are the generations of Jacob
wordNotes.explanation: Toledot comes from yalad, “to beget,” and refers to what is produced by a person: descendants and the history of their family. Each heading in Genesis introduces the story of the next generation rather than the life of the named ancestor himself. So “the generations of Terah” tell of Abraham (Genesis 11:27), and “the generations of Isaac” tell of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:19). Here the account of Jacob’s family will centre on Joseph and his brothers.

wordNotes.term: דִּבָּתָם רָעָה (dibbatam ra‘ah) — their evil report
wordNotes.explanation: Dibbah denotes a report or rumour, usually unfavourable and often slanted. The spies “brought up an evil report” of the land (Numbers 13:32), and the fool “uttereth slander” (Proverbs 10:18). Here the pronoun makes the brothers the subject of the report: Joseph told his father about their bad conduct. The word implies that the brothers regarded such talk as hostile, whatever its accuracy.

verses.bibleText: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children.” The narrator uses the covenant name Israel, a reminder that the father of the twelve tribes carried God’s promise, yet his conduct here does not match the name. Two reasons for the preference are given or implied. The text states that Joseph was “the son of his old age,” born when Jacob was about ninety-one, after the long years of waiting in Haran. Behind that lies the fact that Joseph was the firstborn of Rachel, the wife Jacob had loved from the start (29:18, 30). The language echoes 29:30, where Jacob “loved also Rachel more than Leah.” Love for the mother now flows to the son, with the same dividing effect on the household.

The pattern is painfully familiar. Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob (25:28), and that split set brother against brother, led to deception, and sent Jacob into exile. Jacob had suffered the consequences of parental partiality, yet he repeats it. Sins learned in one generation easily become habits of the next unless grace breaks the cycle (Exodus 20:5-6).

“And he made him a coat of many colours.” The phrase describes a distinctive tunic. The traditional rendering follows the Greek Old Testament, which understood it as a multicoloured garment. The only other place the expression appears is 2 Samuel 13:18-19, where it is the robe worn by the king’s virgin daughters. That suggests a long, ornamented garment, perhaps reaching to the wrists and ankles, the clothing of someone who did not do rough work in the fields. Paintings from Egypt in the early second millennium show Semitic travellers whose chief wears a richly patterned robe, which illustrates the kind of dress Jacob might have given.

Whatever its exact appearance, the robe made a statement. It singled Joseph out as the honoured son and may have signalled that Jacob intended to give him the leadership and double portion that Reuben had forfeited (35:22; 1 Chronicles 5:1-2). In time Joseph did receive the birthright through his two sons (48:5, 22). But a father’s gift meant as love became a badge the brothers could not look at without anger, and the same robe will reappear torn and bloodied at the end of the chapter.

wordNotes.term: כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים (ketonet passim) — coat of many colours
wordNotes.explanation: Ketonet is a tunic, the long inner garment worn by men and women (Genesis 3:21; Exodus 28:4). The qualifying word passim is rare and its meaning uncertain. The Greek Old Testament rendered it “many-coloured,” giving the familiar English. Since pas can refer to the palm or sole, many understand a tunic reaching to the hands and feet, and Daniel uses the Aramaic pas for the part of the hand that wrote on the wall (Daniel 5:5). Its only other use, for the robe of a king’s daughter (2 Samuel 13:18), marks it as a garment of rank.

wordNotes.term: בֶן־זְקֻנִים (ven-zequnim) — the son of his old age
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a son of old age,” from zaqen, “to be old.” The same expression is used of Benjamin, whom Judah calls “a child of his old age” (Genesis 44:20), and Isaac is called the son Sarah bore to Abraham “in his old age” (Genesis 21:2, 7). It emphasizes a child given late in life after long waiting.

verses.bibleText: And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him.” Jacob’s preference was no secret. The verb “saw” stresses that the favouritism was visible, displayed in the robe Joseph wore every day. Their resentment is directed at Joseph himself, though its root lies in their father’s conduct. Hatred often fastens on the favoured person when the one responsible for the favour is out of reach.

They “could not speak peaceably unto him.” The Hebrew reads literally that they were not able to speak to him for peace, which may mean they could not even give him the ordinary greeting, “Peace be to you.” In a culture where the greeting of shalom was the basic courtesy of family life, the refusal to offer it marked a breach. The same word returns with irony in verse 14, when Jacob sends Joseph to see about the “peace” of his brothers.

Scripture traces where such hatred leads. John writes that whoever hates his brother is a murderer at heart (1 John 3:15) and points back to Cain, who refused his brother’s welfare and then killed him (Genesis 4:5-8; 1 John 3:12). Joseph’s brothers are following that same path one step at a time: first they withhold their greeting, then they plot, and finally they sell him. Jesus warned that anger nursed in the heart already breaks the spirit of the sixth commandment (Matthew 5:21-22). The cure is not suppression but a changed heart, and it would take years of guilt and God’s dealings before these brothers came to it (42:21; 50:17).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׂנְאוּ (vayyisne’u) — they hated
wordNotes.explanation: Sane’ ranges from active hostility to being less loved, depending on context. Leah is called “hated” in the sense of being loved less (Genesis 29:31). Here, though, the word is plainly hostile, for it leads to a murder plot. The same verb describes Esau’s attitude to Jacob in a comparable setting of rivalry (Genesis 27:41).

wordNotes.term: דַּבְּרוֹ לְשָׁלֹם (dabbero leshalom) — speak peaceably unto him
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “speak to him for peace.” Shalom means wholeness and wellbeing, and “to speak peace” was to greet someone or to address them in friendship (Esther 10:3; Psalm 28:3). The brothers withheld even this basic courtesy. The word recurs when Jacob sends Joseph to see whether it is “well” (shalom) with them (Genesis 37:14).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it his brethren: and they hated him yet the more.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it his brethren: and they hated him yet the more.” In the ancient world dreams were widely regarded as a channel of revelation, and earlier in Genesis God had spoken through them to Abimelech, to Jacob at Bethel, and to Laban (20:3; 28:12-15; 31:24). Joseph’s dreams differ in that God does not speak in them; they come as pictures whose meaning seems obvious to everyone who hears them. Nothing in the text says plainly that they came from God, but their later fulfilment in Egypt, when the brothers bowed before Joseph again and again (42:6; 43:26; 44:14; 50:18), leaves no room to treat them as the product of a young man’s ambition.

The verb “they hated him yet the more” is a play on Joseph’s name. Yosef means “he adds” (30:24), and here the brothers “added” to their hatred. The same expression closes the paragraph in verse 8, framing the first dream with this growing ill will. Their hatred now has a new cause. The coat showed Jacob’s preference; the dream appeared to show God’s.

That Joseph “told it” to his brothers is central to the plot. He may have been naive, unaware how his words would land, or he may have relished his honour. Either way, the telling deepened the divide. God’s revelations call for wisdom in how and when they are shared, a lesson Joseph would learn well before he stood before Pharaoh.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּחֲלֹם יוֹסֵף חֲלוֹם (vayyachalom yosef chalom) — and Joseph dreamed a dream
wordNotes.explanation: The verb chalam and its noun chalom appear together, a common Hebrew way of emphasis. Dreams carry the plot of the Joseph story: two for Joseph, two for Pharaoh’s servants (Genesis 40:5), and two for Pharaoh (Genesis 41:1-7). God named dreams as one of the ways he spoke to prophets (Numbers 12:6), though they always required testing by his word (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).

verses.bibleText: And he said unto them, Hear, I pray you, this dream which I have dreamed:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said unto them, Hear, I pray you, this dream which I have dreamed.” The request is courteous. The little Hebrew word na softens the command into an appeal, and the narrator lets us hear Joseph’s eagerness to have his brothers listen. Whatever his motives, the boy seems unaware of how fragile the peace in the family has become.

The verse is a pause that heightens the moment before the dream itself is described. A brief note thus has a place in the story: by recording Joseph’s request in full, the narrator puts his openness beside the brothers’ closed hearts. Twenty years later Joseph will again speak to his brothers as they stand before him, and once more they will not understand him, this time because they do not recognise him (42:7-8; 45:3-4).

The courtesy also shows that, whatever his faults, Joseph did not yet regard his brothers as enemies. He wanted them to hear what he had seen. In time the meaning of the dream would bring them bread and life rather than humiliation.

wordNotes.term: שִׁמְעוּ־נָא (shim‘u-na) — hear, I pray you
wordNotes.explanation: An imperative of shama‘, “to hear,” softened by the particle na, which turns a command into a polite request. The same courtesy appears when Abraham addresses the Hittites (Genesis 23:6) and in Joseph’s later appeal to his brothers to come near (Genesis 45:4). Hearing in Hebrew often implies heeding, which is just what the brothers refused to do.

verses.bibleText: For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field.” The opening scene is agricultural. Jacob’s household kept flocks, yet like Isaac before them they also sowed and reaped (26:12; 27:28). Joseph sees all the brothers at work together, tying cut grain into bundles. The thrice-repeated “behold” is typical of dream reports in Genesis (28:12-13; 41:1-3) and gives the account a vivid, step-by-step quality.

“My sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.” The picture needs no interpreter. One sheaf rises and remains standing, while the others gather around it and bow. It does more than rise; it stays upright, a picture of lasting rather than momentary preeminence. In the ancient world prostration before a superior was the normal sign of submission, and the verb used here describes the bow of a subject before a king or a worshipper before God (23:7; 33:3).

The choice of sheaves is fitting in ways the brothers could not have foreseen. The fulfilment came through grain. During the famine they travelled to Egypt to buy food from the governor and “bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth” (42:6), not knowing it was Joseph. The grain he stored in the years of plenty preserved their lives and the life of the promised line (45:7). The dream that sounded like arrogance in a field near Hebron was in fact a promise of deliverance.

The fulfilment also points beyond Joseph. Scripture describes a greater Son before whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10-11). Those who first rejected him will one day acknowledge him, and those who come to him in their need, as the brothers came to Joseph for bread, find in him the Bread of life (John 6:35).

wordNotes.term: אֲלֻמִּים (alummim) — sheaves
wordNotes.explanation: The noun refers to bundles of cut grain bound together at harvest. The psalmist uses it of those who sow in tears and come home rejoicing “bringing his sheaves with him” (Psalm 126:6). Apart from that psalm, it occurs only in this dream, where the sheaves stand for the brothers themselves.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּשְׁתַּחֲוֶיןָ (vattishtachaveyna) — and made obeisance
wordNotes.explanation: A form of the verb usually rendered “bow down” or “worship,” meaning to prostrate oneself. It describes Abraham bowing to the Hittites (Genesis 23:7), Jacob bowing seven times before Esau (Genesis 33:3), and later the brothers bowing before Joseph (Genesis 42:6). The context determines whether it signals respect to a human superior or worship of God.

verses.bibleText: And his brethren said to him, Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us? And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers grasp the meaning at once: “Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?” Each question doubles the verb in Hebrew, a construction that sharpens the tone into scorn: “Do you really think you will be king over us?” They use two words for rule, one tied to kingship and one to authority in general. To them the idea that the second youngest son would govern the family was absurd.

The questions carry irony. Joseph would in fact rule, not merely over his brothers but over all Egypt (41:40-43; 45:8, 26). And the language of kingship anticipates a later question in Israel’s history. Jacob’s final blessings will assign the royal sceptre to Judah (49:10), while Joseph receives the double portion through Ephraim and Manasseh (48:5; 1 Chronicles 5:2). The quarrel over leadership that begins here runs through the history of the tribes.

“And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words.” Their hatred now has two targets: the content of the dreams and the way Joseph told them. Their resistance was ultimately to God, who gave the dreams, though they did not see it that way. The pattern recurs in the Gospels. When Jesus spoke of his kingdom, many responded, “We will not have this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14), and those who refused his rule were often moved by the same envy that drove Joseph’s brothers (Matthew 27:18).

wordNotes.term: הֲמָלֹךְ תִּמְלֹךְ (hamaloch timloch) — shalt thou indeed reign
wordNotes.explanation: The verb malakh, “to be king, reign,” is repeated with an infinitive for emphasis and introduced as a question. The construction can express disbelief or contempt. The parallel phrase uses mashal, “to rule, have dominion,” the verb God used of humanity’s rule over creation in a related sense (Psalm 8:6). Joseph would later describe himself as “ruler” (moshel) throughout the land of Egypt (Genesis 45:8, 26).

verses.bibleText: And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren.” The second dream repeats the message of the first and raises its scope. Later in the story Joseph explains to Pharaoh that a dream given twice means the matter is established by God and will surely come to pass (41:32). The doubling here carries the same weight. What the brothers dismissed once is now confirmed.

The imagery moves from the field to the heavens: “the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me.” In the first dream only the brothers bowed; now the whole household is represented. Jacob understood the sun as himself, the moon as Joseph’s mother, and the eleven stars as the brothers (v. 10). The number eleven matches Jacob’s other sons, including Benjamin, already born at this point (35:16-18).

The stars recall God’s promise to Abraham that his seed would be as countless as the stars of heaven (15:5; 22:17). Jacob’s sons are the beginning of that promised multitude, and the dream shows that God has chosen one of them to preserve the rest. Elsewhere Scripture uses sun, moon, and stars to picture Israel, most memorably in the woman of Revelation 12:1 crowned with twelve stars, who gives birth to the Messiah. Joseph’s dream thus belongs to a larger pattern in which God governs the destiny of his people.

That Joseph again “told it his brethren” after their angry response to the first dream shows a lack of discretion. He was not wrong to have the dream, nor did he invent its meaning, but he had not yet learned when silence serves God’s purpose better than speech.

wordNotes.term: כּוֹכָבִים (kokhavim) — stars
wordNotes.explanation: Kokhav is the ordinary word for a star. God brought Abram outside and invited him to count the stars as a sign of his seed (Genesis 15:5), and Moses later reminded Israel that God had made them as the stars of heaven for multitude (Deuteronomy 1:10). In Joseph’s dream the eleven stars are his brothers, the fathers of that promised people. Balaam’s oracle of a “Star out of Jacob” uses the same word for a coming ruler (Numbers 24:17).

verses.bibleText: And he told it to his father, and to his brethren: and his father rebuked him, and said unto him, What is this dream that thou hast dreamed? Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he told it to his father, and to his brethren.” This time Jacob is present, and the dream concerns him directly. His reaction is a sharp rebuke: “What is this dream that thou hast dreamed? Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth?” In a patriarchal household the thought of a father bowing to his son overturned the natural order. Jacob may also have wanted to distance himself publicly from Joseph’s claims, aware that the brothers already suspected him of favouring Joseph above them.

The mention of “thy mother” raises a question, since Rachel had died giving birth to Benjamin (35:18-19). Jacob may be treating the dream as a picture of the whole family rather than pressing each detail. Alternatively, the moon may represent the woman who had become Joseph’s mother figure, Leah as chief wife or Bilhah as Rachel’s maid. Either way, dreams in Scripture convey their main point through symbols and are not meant to be mapped item by item.

The fulfilment came in stages. The brothers bowed before Joseph several times in Egypt (42:6; 43:26, 28; 44:14). Jacob himself came down to Egypt, and though the text does not record him prostrating himself before Joseph, he placed himself and his family under Joseph’s care and protection (46:29; 47:12). The full scope of the dream was realised as the entire house of Israel depended on Joseph for life.

Jacob’s question, “Shall I … come to bow down,” sounds like a protest, yet as the next verse shows, it did not end his reflection. God sometimes reveals his purposes in ways that offend natural expectations. The Father’s exaltation of the crucified Jesus to universal lordship overturned the world’s ideas of honour even more radically (Acts 2:36; Philippians 2:9).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגְעַר (vayyig‘ar) — and rebuked
wordNotes.explanation: Ga‘ar means to rebuke or reprove sharply. It is used of God rebuking the sea (Psalm 106:9) and of the Lord rebuking Satan (Zechariah 3:2). Jacob’s rebuke expresses disapproval of the dream’s boldness, though the following verse shows that he did not dismiss it. In the New Testament the equivalent Greek verb appears when Jesus rebukes wind and waves (Mark 4:39).

wordNotes.term: לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֺת לְךָ אָרְצָה (lehishtachavot lekha artsah) — to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth
wordNotes.explanation: The addition “to the earth” describes full prostration, face to the ground. It is the posture of Abraham before his heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:2) and of the brothers before Joseph when the dream was fulfilled (Genesis 42:6). Jacob’s phrase shows that he understood the dream to mean the highest form of deference.

verses.bibleText: And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.” Two responses stand side by side. The brothers’ hatred hardens into envy, the resentful longing for what another has. Envy is one of the most destructive of sins because it cannot rejoice in another’s blessing and often turns to violence. Stephen used this very word when he told the Sanhedrin that “the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt” (Acts 7:9), and Pilate recognised that the chief priests had handed Jesus over for the same reason (Mark 15:10).

Jacob’s response is different. Despite his rebuke, he “observed the saying,” that is, he kept it in mind and watched for what would come of it. Perhaps he remembered his own dream at Bethel and the way God had spoken to him in the night (28:12-15; 31:11-13). He could not explain Joseph’s dream, and he did not like what it implied, yet he would not discard it.

The same attitude appears in Mary, who “kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart” after the shepherds’ visit and again after Jesus spoke in the temple (Luke 2:19, 51). Daniel likewise “kept the matter” in his heart after a vision he did not fully understand (Daniel 7:28). There is wisdom in holding on to what God has shown even when its meaning is not yet clear. Jacob would wait more than twenty years before he saw the dream fulfilled.

wordNotes.term: וַיְקַנְאוּ־בוֹ (vayqanne’u-vo) — envied him
wordNotes.explanation: Qana’ in the Piel describes jealousy or envy, a passionate response to another’s advantage. Rachel envied her sister’s fruitfulness (Genesis 30:1), and the Philistines envied Isaac’s prosperity (Genesis 26:14). The same root can also describe God’s holy zeal for his people (Exodus 20:5), but here it is wholly sinful. The Septuagint renders it with the verb Stephen echoes in Acts 7:9.

wordNotes.term: שָׁמַר אֶת־הַדָּבָר (shamar et-haddavar) — observed the saying
wordNotes.explanation: Shamar means to guard, keep, or watch over. With davar, “word, matter,” it means to keep something in mind and wait for its outcome. The Greek of Luke 2:51, describing Mary keeping Jesus’s sayings in her heart, uses language very close to the Septuagint here. The phrase describes thoughtful attention rather than mere memory.

verses.bibleText: And his brethren went to feed their father's flock in Shechem.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And his brethren went to feed their father’s flock in Shechem.” The second movement of the chapter begins with a change of scene. The brothers take the flocks some fifty miles north of Hebron to the pastures around Shechem. Herdsmen in Canaan moved their animals seasonally, and the northern hill country offered better grazing in the dry months between spring and autumn. Jacob also owned a parcel of land near Shechem, bought from the sons of Hamor (33:19).

The name Shechem would have stirred uneasy memories. It was there that Simeon and Levi slaughtered the men of the city after the violation of Dinah, and the brothers plundered it (34:25-29). Jacob had feared reprisals from the surrounding peoples (34:30), and only God’s protection had kept the family safe as they left (35:5). That the brothers return there suggests both confidence and indifference to the past. It also helps explain why Jacob is anxious about them in the next verse.

Joseph has stayed behind in Hebron, and the distance between the brothers and their father’s house will soon leave them free to act without restraint.

wordNotes.term: שְׁכֶם (shekhem) — Shechem
wordNotes.explanation: The name means “shoulder,” perhaps referring to the city’s position on the slope between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. Abraham built his first altar in Canaan there (Genesis 12:6-7), and Jacob bought land and erected an altar nearby (Genesis 33:18-20). Joseph’s bones would one day be buried at Shechem in that same field (Joshua 24:32), so the district where his betrayal began became his final resting place.

verses.bibleText: And Israel said unto Joseph, Do not thy brethren feed the flock in Shechem? come, and I will send thee unto them. And he said to him, Here am I.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel said unto Joseph, Do not thy brethren feed the flock in Shechem? come, and I will send thee unto them.” Jacob’s concern is understandable. His sons are far away, near a city they had plundered, and no news has come. What he seems not to grasp is the depth of their hostility toward Joseph. Either the brothers had kept their hatred hidden from their father, or Jacob, blinded by affection, could not imagine that it would lead to harm. He sends his favourite son alone, perhaps still wearing the distinctive robe, into the hands of those who resented him most.

Joseph’s reply is simple: “Here am I.” The Hebrew hinneni expresses readiness to listen and obey. It is the answer Abraham gave when God called him to offer Isaac (22:1, 11), the answer Moses gave at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4), and the answer Isaiah gave in the temple (Isaiah 6:8). Joseph does not hesitate, though he knows how his brothers feel about him. His obedience to his father is unconditional.

The scene also foreshadows a greater sending. In the parable of the vineyard Jesus describes a father who, after sending many servants, finally sends his beloved son, saying, “They will reverence my son” (Mark 12:6). The tenants instead see the heir as a threat and kill him. Jesus applied that story to himself and the leaders who rejected him. The heavenly Father sent his Son knowing full well what awaited him, and the Son came willingly (John 3:16; Hebrews 10:7). Joseph’s journey to his brothers offers a faint outline of that mission, though Jacob sent his son in ignorance and God sent his Son in full foreknowledge and love.

wordNotes.term: הִנֵּנִי (hinneni) — here am I
wordNotes.explanation: The particle hinneh, “behold,” with the first-person suffix: “behold me.” It signals attentive readiness to respond to a call. Abraham uses it three times in Genesis 22 (vv. 1, 7, 11), Jacob uses it when God calls him in a night vision (Genesis 46:2), and young Samuel uses it in the temple (1 Samuel 3:4). On Joseph’s lips it marks willing obedience to his father.

verses.bibleText: And he said to him, Go, I pray thee, see whether it be well with thy brethren, and well with the flocks; and bring me word again. So he sent him out of the vale of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Go, I pray thee, see whether it be well with thy brethren, and well with the flocks; and bring me word again.” Twice Jacob uses the word shalom, “well-being.” The irony is sharp. The brothers had been unable to speak shalom to Joseph (v. 4), yet he is sent to inquire about theirs. Jacob wants to know that his sons and his flocks are safe, and he asks Joseph to bring back a report. To brothers who remembered the evil report of verse 2, his arrival could easily look like one more errand of supervision.

“So he sent him out of the vale of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.” Hebron lies in a valley in the hill country of Judah, the region where Abraham had lived by the oaks of Mamre and where he, Sarah, and later Isaac and Jacob were buried in the cave of Machpelah (23:19; 35:27). From there to Shechem was a journey of several days on foot. Joseph left behind the security of his father’s house.

He would not see Hebron again for many years, and Jacob would not see him for more than twenty. The vale of Hebron, associated with the promises to the fathers, is the starting point of a road that will lead through slavery and prison to the throne of Egypt. God had told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in a land not theirs (15:13), and with this sending the first step toward that sojourn is taken, though no one in the story yet knows it.

wordNotes.term: שְׁלוֹם אַחֶיךָ (shelom achekha) — whether it be well with thy brethren
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the peace of your brothers.” Shalom here means general welfare and safety. Asking after someone’s shalom was a customary greeting and inquiry (Genesis 29:6; 43:27). Jesse sends young David to check on his brothers’ welfare in strikingly similar language (1 Samuel 17:18), and in both stories the youngest son sent with care meets scorn from his older brothers.

wordNotes.term: עֵמֶק חֶבְרוֹן (‘emeq chevron) — the vale of Hebron
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Emeq is a broad valley or lowland. Hebron, also known as Kiriath-arba, sits among the hills of Judah and was closely tied to the patriarchs (Genesis 13:18; 23:2). It later became one of the cities of refuge and David’s first royal city (Joshua 20:7; 2 Samuel 2:1-4).

verses.bibleText: And a certain man found him, and, behold, he was wandering in the field: and the man asked him, saying, What seekest thou?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And a certain man found him, and, behold, he was wandering in the field.” Joseph reaches Shechem but cannot find his brothers. The pastures are empty. A young man far from home, he walks aimlessly through the countryside. At this point an unnamed man meets him and asks, “What seekest thou?”

The narrator does not say who the man is, and nothing else is told about him. His appearance seems incidental, yet the story depends on it. Without his help Joseph might have returned home with no news, the brothers would have stayed at Dothan without him, and the caravan would have passed unseen. Instead the stranger knows exactly where the brothers have gone. Ancient Jewish interpreters sometimes saw an angel in him, but the text is content to call him “a man,” and that restraint is part of its message. God frequently works through ordinary people and seemingly chance encounters (Ruth 2:3; Proverbs 16:9).

The image of Joseph “wandering” is suggestive. The same verb is used of sheep that go astray (Psalm 119:176; Isaiah 53:6), and of Hagar wandering in the wilderness of Beersheba (21:14). Joseph, the shepherd boy, is himself lost and must be guided. In the larger story he is not truly lost, for every step is under God’s direction (Psalm 37:23).

wordNotes.term: תֹעֶה (to‘eh) — wandering
wordNotes.explanation: A participle of ta‘ah, “to wander, go astray.” It describes physical straying, like Hagar in the desert (Genesis 21:14), and is often used figuratively of moral straying (Psalm 119:176; Isaiah 53:6). Here it portrays Joseph searching without direction until the stranger points the way.

verses.bibleText: And he said, I seek my brethren: tell me, I pray thee, where they feed their flocks.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, I seek my brethren: tell me, I pray thee, where they feed their flocks.” Joseph’s answer is direct and courteous. In Hebrew the object stands first for emphasis: “My brothers I am seeking.” He speaks of them as “my brethren” even though they had refused to speak peaceably to him.

Read in the light of the whole story, the words have a meaning beyond the moment. Cain had asked, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (4:9). Joseph, sent by his father, is his brothers’ seeker. Years later in Egypt he will seek them again, testing their hearts and then revealing himself to bring them to repentance and reconciliation (42:9-17; 45:1-5). Joseph’s whole career can be summed up in this sentence.

The Gospels show a greater Brother who came seeking. Jesus described his mission as coming “to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10), and he called those who do the Father’s will his brothers (Matthew 12:50). Hebrews says he is not ashamed to call them brethren (Hebrews 2:11).

wordNotes.term: אֶת־אַחַי אָנֹכִי מְבַקֵּשׁ (et-achai anokhi mevaqqesh) — I seek my brethren
wordNotes.explanation: The participle of baqash, “to seek,” describes ongoing action: “I am looking for my brothers.” The fronted object gives emphasis to “my brothers.” The verb often describes earnest searching (Deuteronomy 4:29). The kinship term ach, “brother,” is a keyword of the chapter, appearing more than a dozen times and underlining the tragedy of brothers betraying a brother.

verses.bibleText: And the man said, They are departed hence; for I heard them say, Let us go to Dothan. And Joseph went after his brethren, and found them in Dothan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the man said, They are departed hence; for I heard them say, Let us go to Dothan.” The stranger had overheard the brothers’ plans, another detail that seems accidental but proves decisive. Dothan lay some thirteen to fifteen miles north and west of Shechem, on the edge of a fertile plain with good grazing. More importantly, it stood beside the main trade route that ran from Gilead across the Jordan valley, through the plain of Jezreel, and down the coast to Egypt. Had the brothers remained at Shechem, no caravan would have passed them.

“And Joseph went after his brethren, and found them in Dothan.” His perseverance is notable. He had already travelled about fifty miles; now he goes farther from home and from any help his father might give. The verb “found” echoes verse 15: the man “found” Joseph, and now Joseph “finds” his brothers. But what he finds is not a welcome.

Centuries later Dothan was the scene of another story of providence. When the king of Syria sent an army to capture Elisha there, the prophet prayed that his servant’s eyes would be opened, and the young man saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:13-17). Joseph saw no such vision at Dothan, yet the same God was guarding him. Joseph would later confess that it was God, not his brothers, who sent him to Egypt (45:8).

The chain of small events deserves attention. Had Joseph found his brothers at Shechem, he would have been far from the trade road; had he reached Dothan a day later, the caravan might already have gone by. A few overheard words, a stranger’s willingness to help, and a young man’s persistence all fall into place. Scripture rarely explains such moments while they are happening, yet it teaches that many plans arise in a human heart while the counsel of the LORD is what stands (Proverbs 19:21).

wordNotes.term: דֹּתָיְנָה (dotayenah) — to Dothan
wordNotes.explanation: The name Dothan appears with a directional ending, “toward Dothan.” The site, identified with Tell Dothan north of Shechem, was occupied in the patriarchal period and lay on a natural pass used by traders. Apart from this chapter it appears only in the Elisha story (2 Kings 6:13), where God protects his servant from a surrounding army.

verses.bibleText: And when they saw him afar off, even before he came near unto them, they conspired against him to slay him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when they saw him afar off, even before he came near unto them, they conspired against him to slay him.” The brothers recognise Joseph at a distance, perhaps by the robe. By the time he reaches them they have already decided to kill him. The narrator emphasises the speed with which their hatred becomes murderous intent. There is no confrontation, no debate about his errand, no attempt to hear him. The decision is made before a word is spoken.

The verb “conspired” suggests crafty, deceitful planning. It is used of the Midianites who plotted against Israel through the matter of Peor (Numbers 25:18) and of the Egyptians whom God turned to “deal subtilly with his servants” (Psalm 105:25). The same malice that will later oppress Israel in Egypt is at work first within Israel’s own family.

The Gospels record a similar resolution. After Jesus raised Lazarus, the council “took counsel together for to put him to death” (John 11:53), and the chief priests and elders “consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him” (Matthew 26:3-4). In both stories the beloved son approaches in peace while those who should welcome him are already plotting his death. The parallel is not a detail-by-detail allegory, but it shows a recurring pattern in which God’s chosen one is rejected by his own (John 1:11).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתְנַכְּלוּ (vayyitnakkelu) — they conspired
wordNotes.explanation: The Hithpael of nakhal, “to be crafty, deceitful,” means to plot cunningly against someone. The related noun nekhel describes the “wiles” of the Midianites (Numbers 25:18). Psalm 105:25 uses the same verb of the Egyptians’ scheming against Israel. The word implies premeditated malice rather than sudden rage.

verses.bibleText: And they said one to another, Behold, this dreamer cometh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they said one to another, Behold, this dreamer cometh.” The Hebrew phrase is literally “this master of dreams.” It is a sneer, mocking Joseph as a specialist in grand visions. They do not call him by name or describe him as their brother. What offends them most is not the report or even the robe, but the dreams, which threaten their place in the family.

Their mockery proves prophetic. Joseph will indeed become a master of dreams. In prison he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh’s butler and baker (40:8-22), and before Pharaoh he explains the dreams of the fat and lean cattle, insisting that the interpretation belongs to God (41:16, 25). The very gift they despised will save their lives.

The description of Joseph as “this dreamer” also recalls a later warning. The law of Moses commanded Israel to reject a “dreamer of dreams” who led people after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). Joseph’s dreams, by contrast, pointed to the fulfilment of God’s purposes. Scripture tests every message by its fruit and its faithfulness to God.

wordNotes.term: בַּעַל הַחֲלֹמוֹת (ba‘al hachalomot) — this dreamer
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the lord of the dreams.” Ba‘al means “owner, master, lord” and, with a following noun, describes someone characterized by that thing, as in “a hairy man” (literally “a lord of hair,” 2 Kings 1:8). Here the phrase drips with sarcasm. The demonstrative “this” is also scornful, as when Israel later says, “this Moses” (Exodus 32:1).

verses.bibleText: Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit, and we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him: and we shall see what will become of his dreams.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit.” The plan is spoken aloud in a rush of verbs: come, kill, throw. The land around Dothan was dotted with cisterns cut into the rock to catch winter rain. In summer many stood dry, and a body dropped into one would never be found. The verb for “slay” is the one used when Cain rose up against Abel and killed him (4:8). The brothers who should have been Joseph’s keepers now take Cain’s path.

Their cover story is ready: “Some evil beast hath devoured him.” In the hill country of the second millennium lions and bears were a real danger to shepherds and travellers (Judges 14:5; 1 Samuel 17:34-36; 1 Kings 13:24). A young man alone on the road could easily be killed, and Jacob would have no reason to suspect his sons. Once they had stained their hands with the blood of Shechem’s men (34:25-26), the step to fratricide seemed less unthinkable.

The climax of their speech reveals their deepest motive: “and we shall see what will become of his dreams.” They intend to put God’s revealed purpose to the test and defeat it by killing the one through whom it was to be fulfilled. The irony is that their efforts to destroy the dreams become the means of fulfilling them. The psalmist could later look back and say that God “sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant” (Psalm 105:17).

Jesus put words very like these into the mouths of the tenants in his parable: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours” (Mark 12:7). The leaders who heard it recognised that he spoke of them (Mark 12:12). As with Joseph, those who sought to put an end to the Son’s claims became unwitting agents of God’s plan, for the rejected stone became the head of the corner (Psalm 118:22-23; Acts 4:10-11).

wordNotes.term: בּוֹר (bor) — pit
wordNotes.explanation: A cistern or pit dug or hewn in rock for storing water. When dry, such pits served as prisons (Jeremiah 38:6) or as places to dispose of bodies (Jeremiah 41:7, 9). The word reappears when Joseph later calls his prison in Egypt “the dungeon” (Genesis 40:15). In poetry the “pit” often stands for death or the grave (Psalm 28:1; 30:3).

wordNotes.term: חַיָּה רָעָה (chayyah ra‘ah) — evil beast
wordNotes.explanation: Chayyah means a living creature, and with ra‘ah, “evil, harmful,” it means a dangerous wild animal. God threatened Israel with “evil beasts” among the covenant curses (Ezekiel 14:15; Leviticus 26:6, 22). The brothers’ phrase will be repeated by Jacob himself when he recognises the robe (Genesis 37:33), showing how completely their lie succeeds.

verses.bibleText: And Reuben heard it, and he delivered him out of their hands; and said, Let us not kill him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reuben heard it, and he delivered him out of their hands; and said, Let us not kill him.” Reuben, the eldest, intervenes. That he “heard it” may suggest he had not been part of the first conversation, or simply that he responded once the plan was voiced. As firstborn he bore particular responsibility toward his father and his brothers. He had already shamed Jacob by lying with Bilhah (35:22), and some think he hoped to regain his father’s favour by saving Joseph. The text records his action without explaining his motive.

The narrator says he “delivered him out of their hands,” then reports his words. The statement anticipates the result of the following verses. Reuben does not refute their hatred or defend Joseph’s innocence. He proposes a lesser evil that leaves the outcome open. He is decent enough to want to rescue Joseph, but not strong enough to oppose his brothers openly. Jacob would later describe him as “unstable as water” (49:4), and his conduct here fits that judgment.

His words translate literally as “Let us not strike him in respect of life,” using nephesh, which here plainly means Joseph’s life. Hebrew speaks this way frequently: to “smite the nephesh” is to take a person’s life (Leviticus 24:17; Deuteronomy 19:6). The word refers to the living person, not to a separable immortal entity within him. Reuben’s appeal is simple: do not kill him. It would be years before he could remind his brothers that he had told them not to sin against the child (42:22).

wordNotes.term: וַיַּצִּלֵהוּ (vayyatsilehu) — and he delivered him
wordNotes.explanation: The Hiphil of natsal, “to snatch away, rescue.” It describes pulling someone out of danger, as when God delivered Israel from the hand of Egypt (Exodus 3:8; 18:10). Here it expresses Reuben’s intention and first step rather than final success, since he fails to restore Joseph to his father. The verb recurs at the end of verse 22.

wordNotes.term: לֹא נַכֶּנּוּ נָפֶשׁ (lo nakkennu nafesh) — let us not kill him
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “let us not smite him as to life.” Nephesh here means life itself, the vitality of a living person. The same expression appears in the laws about manslaughter: one who “smiteth him mortally” (Deuteronomy 19:6, 11). This usage confirms that nephesh in Scripture refers to the person as a living being rather than to an immortal component.

verses.bibleText: And Reuben said unto them, Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and lay no hand upon him; that he might rid him out of their hands, to deliver him to his father again.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reuben said unto them, Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and lay no hand upon him.” Reuben appeals to the gravest of taboos. From the days of Noah God had declared that whoever sheds man’s blood would answer for it, because humans are made in God’s image (9:5-6). Abel’s blood had cried out from the ground (4:10). To shed a brother’s blood was to invite God’s judgment.

His alternative is a dry cistern “in the wilderness,” which here means open grazing country away from settlements, where no one would hear Joseph’s cries. Reuben presents it as a way to let Joseph die without directly killing him. To the others the difference may have seemed slight. A man left in a dry pit would perish of thirst and exposure just as surely, but they could tell themselves their hands were clean.

The narrator then reveals Reuben’s real intention: “that he might rid him out of their hands, to deliver him to his father again.” He planned to return secretly and rescue Joseph. The plan was well meant, but it rested on deception rather than open confrontation, and it depended on Reuben’s being present at the right moment. His absence when the caravan arrived would leave the plan in ruins. Good intentions without the courage to act on them openly can leave the innocent unprotected.

wordNotes.term: אַל־תִּשְׁפְּכוּ־דָם (al-tishpekhu-dam) — shed no blood
wordNotes.explanation: Shaphakh means “to pour out.” “To pour out blood” is the standard Hebrew expression for murder, first used in God’s covenant with Noah: “Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Genesis 9:6). Moses later warned that shed blood defiles the land (Numbers 35:33). Reuben’s plea appeals to this ancient principle.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him.” Joseph’s arrival is reported without any greeting from either side. His long journey ends, and his brothers seize him. The first thing they do is tear off the robe. The narrator lingers over the garment, naming it twice: “his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him.” This is the symbol of everything they resent, the visible token of their father’s favour and of Joseph’s claim to preeminence.

Stripping someone of his clothing was a common way to humiliate and dishonour. Taking the robe meant taking away Joseph’s status and reducing him to the level of a slave. The verb is used for stripping a defeated enemy or a slain warrior (1 Samuel 31:8-9). In the story of Joseph clothing marks every reversal of his fortunes: he loses this robe to his brothers, his garment to Potiphar’s wife (39:12), and his prison clothes when he is called before Pharaoh, who then dresses him in fine linen (41:14, 42).

The scene foreshadows the way Christ was treated. Before his crucifixion the soldiers stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him in mockery (Matthew 27:28). At the cross they divided his garments and cast lots for his seamless coat, fulfilling Psalm 22:18 (John 19:23-24). Joseph was stripped and later exalted and robed in honour, and Christ was stripped and humiliated, then raised and exalted by the Father (Philippians 2:8-9).

wordNotes.term: וַיַּפְשִׁיטוּ (vayyafshitu) — they stript
wordNotes.explanation: The Hiphil of pashat, “to strip off.” It is used of removing garments, sometimes in a priestly setting where Aaron is stripped of his vestments before his death (Numbers 20:26, 28) and sometimes of plundering the dead (1 Samuel 31:9). Here it describes the violent removal of the symbol of Joseph’s privilege, an act of dishonour.

verses.bibleText: And they took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it.” The narration is spare. The brothers adopt Reuben’s proposal, though their purpose is not his. They throw Joseph alive into the dry cistern. The additional detail that “there was no water in it” explains why Joseph did not drown, but it also stresses the cruelty of the act. With no water he would die of thirst under the summer sun.

The narrator says nothing here about Joseph’s reaction. That silence is filled in later, when the brothers confess to one another in Egypt: “We saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear” (42:21). Joseph pleaded with them from the pit, and they ignored him. The memory haunted them for more than twenty years.

In Hebrew poetry the pit becomes an image of death, deep distress, and abandonment. The psalmist cries, “Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness” (Psalm 88:6), and rejoices that God “brought me up also out of an horrible pit” (Psalm 40:2). Zechariah foresees the Lord setting his prisoners free from the “pit wherein is no water” by the blood of his covenant (Zechariah 9:11). Joseph’s waterless cistern became a place where God’s care was hidden but not absent. Like Jeremiah lowered into the mud of a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6), he was not forgotten.

Psalm 105 adds a detail that Genesis leaves for later chapters: Joseph’s feet were hurt with fetters and he was laid in iron “until the time that his word came,” while the word of the LORD tried him (Psalm 105:18-19). The pit at Dothan was the first stage of that testing. The boy who had spoken so freely of his dreams now had nothing left except the God who had given them. Genesis records no complaint from Joseph against God, and when he finally speaks of these events he traces God’s hand in them (45:5-8). Suffering became the school in which his character was refined.

wordNotes.term: וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם (vehabbor req en bo mayim) — the pit was empty, there was no water in it
wordNotes.explanation: Req means “empty, void.” The doubled statement, “empty” and “no water,” emphasizes the dryness of the cistern. Zechariah uses almost the same language for the dungeon from which God will release his prisoners (Zechariah 9:11). The cistern into which Jeremiah was lowered, by contrast, had no water but held mud (Jeremiah 38:6).

verses.bibleText: And they sat down to eat bread: and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they sat down to eat bread.” The brothers’ callousness is stark. Their brother is in the pit, pleading for his life, and they sit down to a meal. Amos later rebuked those who feasted at ease while caring nothing for “the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6:4-6), and the phrase likely echoes this very scene. The next time these brothers eat in Joseph’s presence will be in Egypt, at a meal he provides, seated in birth order to their astonishment (43:32-34).

“And they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead.” The phrase “lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold” often signals a moment when God’s provision comes into view (18:2; 22:13). Here it introduces a caravan of traders. The road through Dothan was part of the main route from the east to Egypt, crossing the Jordan from Gilead, passing through the valley of Jezreel, and continuing down the coastal plain. Traders using camels carried goods over long distances, and spices were among the most valuable cargo.

The cargo is listed precisely: “spicery and balm and myrrh.” These aromatic resins came from shrubs and trees in Gilead and beyond and were prized in Egypt for medicine, perfume, incense, and embalming. Gilead’s balm was famous; Jeremiah would later ask, “Is there no balm in Gilead?” (Jeremiah 8:22). Years later Jacob would send the same products to Egypt as a gift to win the governor’s favour, not knowing that the governor was Joseph (43:11).

The caravan’s timing is not coincidence. Joseph was found by the man in Shechem, guided to Dothan, thrown into the pit, and now, just as the brothers sit down to eat, traders appear on the road. God was arranging the details so that what the brothers intended for evil would bring Joseph to Egypt (50:20).

wordNotes.term: אֹרְחַת יִשְׁמְעֵאלִים (orchat yishme‘elim) — a company of Ishmeelites
wordNotes.explanation: ’Orchah, from ’arach, “to travel,” means a travelling company or caravan (Job 6:19; Isaiah 21:13). The Ishmaelites were descendants of Abraham’s son Ishmael, who lived in the wilderness regions south and east of Canaan (Genesis 25:12-18). The term seems to have become a general name for desert traders as well as an ethnic designation.

wordNotes.term: נְכֹאת וּצְרִי וָלֹט (nekho’t utseri valot) — spicery and balm and myrrh
wordNotes.explanation: These are three aromatic resins whose exact identification is uncertain. Nekho’t may be gum tragacanth; tseri is the famous balm of Gilead, a resin valued for healing (Jeremiah 46:11); lot is probably ladanum, the fragrant gum of the rockrose, rather than true myrrh. Jacob later sends “a little balm … spices, and myrrh” to Egypt (Genesis 43:11).

verses.bibleText: And Judah said unto his brethren, What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Judah said unto his brethren, What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood?” Judah, the fourth son of Leah, now takes the lead. His question is practical rather than moral. The word for “profit” usually refers to gain, often dishonest gain (Exodus 18:21; Proverbs 1:19). Judah reasons that killing Joseph would bring them nothing.

The expression “conceal his blood” reflects the ancient conviction that innocent blood cries out to God for justice even when it is covered. God told Cain that Abel’s blood was crying from the ground (4:10), and Job prayed, “O earth, cover not thou my blood” (Job 16:18). Judah may have sensed that no concealment could hide such a crime from God.

Still, his argument is a mixture of conscience and calculation. His solution will remove Joseph from the family just as effectively as death. Later, when Benjamin’s freedom is at stake, this same Judah will offer himself as a slave in his brother’s place (44:33). The man who here sells a brother for profit will one day give himself for a brother out of love, and from his tribe would come the Lion of Judah who gave himself for all (Genesis 49:10; Revelation 5:5).

wordNotes.term: מַה־בֶּצַע (mah-betsa‘) — what profit
wordNotes.explanation: Betsa‘ means “gain, profit,” often with the nuance of ill-gotten gain. Jethro advised Moses to appoint judges who hated “covetousness” (betsa‘, Exodus 18:21), and Proverbs warns of those greedy of gain (Proverbs 1:19). Judah’s question frames the decision in terms of advantage rather than right and wrong.

wordNotes.term: וְכִסִּינוּ אֶת־דָּמוֹ (vekhissinu et-damo) — and conceal his blood
wordNotes.explanation: The Piel of kasah, “to cover.” Covering blood was a way of hiding guilt, yet Scripture insists that God sees it. Ezekiel describes blood set on a bare rock so that it cannot be covered and cries for vengeance (Ezekiel 24:7-8). Judah’s phrase admits that leaving Joseph to die would still be bloodshed.

verses.bibleText: Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother and our flesh. And his brethren were content.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother and our flesh.” Judah’s proposal is to turn Joseph into merchandise. The brothers would be rid of him, avoid the guilt of bloodshed, and make money at the same time. His words reveal a troubling double standard. He appeals to kinship, “he is our brother and our flesh,” yet uses that kinship to argue for selling him rather than saving him. The phrase echoes Laban’s words to Jacob, “thou art my bone and my flesh” (29:14), which had preceded his own exploitation of his nephew.

The law later given at Sinai would treat Judah’s plan as a capital crime: “He that stealeth a man, and selleth him … he shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7). Kidnapping and slave-trading violated the dignity of a person made in God’s image. Paul lists “menstealers” among those whose conduct the law condemns (1 Timothy 1:10), and Amos would later indict Israel for selling the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes (Amos 2:6). The principle was already true before Sinai, for the brothers’ own consciences later accused them (42:21).

“And his brethren were content.” Literally, “his brothers listened.” They agreed. The same verb that described Joseph’s appeal to them to “hear” his dream (v. 6) now describes their willingness to hear Judah’s plan. They would not listen to Joseph’s dreams or to his pleas from the pit, but they listened to the proposal to sell him. Yet God, who works even through such choices, would use this decision to preserve both Joseph and the brothers themselves (45:5-7).

wordNotes.term: אָחִינוּ בְשָׂרֵנוּ (achinu vesarenu) — our brother and our flesh
wordNotes.explanation: Basar, “flesh,” used with family terms expresses close kinship. Laban called Jacob “my bone and my flesh” (Genesis 29:14), and Isaiah urged Israel not to hide from “thine own flesh,” meaning one’s needy kin (Isaiah 58:7). Judah’s appeal to kinship is used to justify a lesser crime rather than to protect his brother.

verses.bibleText: Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver.” The verse moves quickly. As the caravan approaches, the brothers haul Joseph up from the cistern and sell him. The repetition of Joseph’s name three times in the Hebrew sentence slows the reader, like a bell tolling over a solemn event: they drew up Joseph, sold Joseph, and brought Joseph into Egypt.

The traders are called both “Midianites” and “Ishmeelites.” Some have proposed that these names point to two separate groups or two versions of the story, but the text itself treats them as the same caravan. Midian and Ishmael were both sons of Abraham through Keturah and Hagar (25:2, 12), and their descendants lived in the same desert regions. In Judges 8:24 the Midianites defeated by Gideon are described as Ishmaelites because they wore gold earrings, which shows that the name could be used broadly for nomadic traders. Verse 36 says the Midianites sold Joseph to Potiphar, while 39:1 says Potiphar bought him from the Ishmaelites. Both refer to one transaction. Joseph’s later words, “I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt” (45:4), confirm that the brothers themselves sold him.

The price was “twenty pieces of silver,” that is, twenty shekels. Ancient Near Eastern texts from the early second millennium show this as a typical price for a slave, and the law of Moses later set twenty shekels as the valuation of a male between five and twenty years old (Leviticus 27:5).

Joseph’s sale for silver recalls another betrayal. Judas, whose name is the Greek form of Judah, agreed to deliver Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14-16; Zechariah 11:12-13). Stephen, recounting Israel’s history before the Sanhedrin, told how the patriarchs sold Joseph out of envy, “but God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions” (Acts 7:9-10). His listeners would soon reject Stephen as their fathers had rejected Joseph and as they themselves had rejected Christ.

The parallel should not be pressed into every detail. In both cases a beloved son was hated without cause, betrayed for silver by those who should have honoured him, and handed over to Gentiles. In both cases God turned the betrayal into the means of salvation. Joseph was brought to Egypt as a slave and became the saviour of his family and of the nations; Jesus was delivered up and became the Saviour of the world (Acts 2:23-24, 36).

wordNotes.term: עֶשְׂרִים כָּסֶף (‘esrim kasef) — twenty pieces of silver
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “twenty of silver,” with shekel understood. The shekel was a unit of weight, roughly eleven grams, rather than a coin. Leviticus later set twenty shekels as the value of a male aged five to twenty (Leviticus 27:5), and Exodus fixed thirty shekels as compensation for a slave (Exodus 21:32). Zechariah’s “thirty pieces of silver,” the price of the rejected shepherd (Zechariah 11:12), is quoted of Judas’s bargain in Matthew 27:9.

wordNotes.term: מִדְיָנִים סֹחֲרִים (midyanim socharim) — Midianites merchantmen
wordNotes.explanation: Socharim are traders who travel about to buy and sell, from sachar, “to go around.” The same word describes the merchants of Tarshish and Tyre (Isaiah 23:2, 8). The Midianites descended from Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2, 4). Judges 8:22-24 shows that “Midianites” and “Ishmaelites” could name the same people.

verses.bibleText: And Reuben returned unto the pit; and, behold, Joseph was not in the pit; and he rent his clothes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reuben returned unto the pit; and, behold, Joseph was not in the pit; and he rent his clothes.” Reuben had not been present when Joseph was sold. Perhaps he had gone to tend the flocks, or had deliberately withdrawn to avoid suspicion while he waited for an opportunity to rescue Joseph. Either way, his absence at the decisive moment ruined his plan.

He returns to find the pit empty, and he tears his clothes. Rending garments was the customary sign of grief and shock in the ancient Near East. Jacob will do the same when he sees the robe (v. 34), the brothers will tear their clothes when the cup is found in Benjamin’s sack (44:13), and Job tore his robe when he heard of his children’s death (Job 1:20). Reuben’s grief is sincere, but it comes too late.

The empty pit is a moment of despair for Reuben, yet in the larger story it marks the beginning of Joseph’s rescue. What Reuben saw as disaster was, in God’s design, the way of preservation. There is a faint anticipation here of another empty place that seemed at first to signal loss. The women who came to Jesus’s tomb found it empty and were perplexed, until they learned that he was alive (Luke 24:2-6).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְרַע אֶת־בְּגָדָיו (vayyiqra‘ et-begadav) — and he rent his clothes
wordNotes.explanation: Qara‘ means “to tear.” Tearing one’s garments expressed grief, horror, or repentance (2 Samuel 1:11; 2 Kings 22:11). Joel calls God’s people to “rend your heart, and not your garments” (Joel 2:13), showing that the outward sign was meant to reflect inward sorrow. Reuben’s action is the first such mourning gesture in Scripture.

verses.bibleText: And he returned unto his brethren, and said, The child is not; and I, whither shall I go?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he returned unto his brethren, and said, The child is not; and I, whither shall I go?” Reuben’s words break out in short, anguished phrases. “The child is not” means he is gone, vanished. Reuben calls Joseph “the child,” a term of tenderness that also points to Joseph’s youth and vulnerability. The same expression, “is not,” is used of Enoch, who “was not, for God took him” (5:24), and Jacob will use it of Joseph and Simeon when he believes both are lost (42:13, 36).

“And I, whither shall I go?” As the eldest, Reuben would have to answer to his father. He had already disgraced himself through his sin with Bilhah, and now he has failed to protect the son his father loved most. He has no plan and no means of setting things right.

The brothers give him no answer. Only years later, when the brothers are in trouble in Egypt, will Reuben remind them, “Spake I not unto you, saying, Do not sin against the child; and ye would not hear?” (42:22). Later still he will offer his own sons as surety for Benjamin (42:37). Reuben’s good intentions consistently fall short of decisive action.

wordNotes.term: הַיֶּלֶד אֵינֶנּוּ (hayyeled enennu) — the child is not
wordNotes.explanation: ’Enennu, “he is not,” states that a person is absent or no longer alive. It is used of Enoch’s removal (Genesis 5:24) and of Jacob’s lament, “Joseph is not, and Simeon is not” (Genesis 42:36). Jeremiah’s picture of Rachel weeping for her children “because they were not” uses the same idiom (Jeremiah 31:15). Yeled, “child,” stresses Joseph’s youth.

verses.bibleText: And they took Joseph's coat, and killed a kid of the goats, and dipped the coat in the blood;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they took Joseph’s coat, and killed a kid of the goats, and dipped the coat in the blood.” The brothers move swiftly to cover their crime. They take the robe they had stripped from Joseph, slaughter a young goat, and soak the garment in its blood. Goat’s blood would look much like human blood, and the robe, which Jacob knew so well, would serve as unmistakable evidence.

The irony is deep. Years earlier Jacob had deceived his own father with the skins of two kids of the goats and the borrowed garments of Esau (27:9, 15-16). Isaac, blind and old, had been fooled by the feel of goat hair and the smell of clothing. Now Jacob’s sons use a goat and a garment to deceive him. The pattern is too precise to be accidental. Scripture does not say that God planned this as punishment, but it shows that “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Jacob’s earlier sin returns to him through his own children.

The goat also points ahead to Israel’s worship. Under the law a kid of the goats was offered as a sin offering, and on the Day of Atonement the blood of a goat was carried into the most holy place to make atonement (Leviticus 16:15). In Genesis 37 the blood of a goat serves a lie; in the sanctuary it would point to the truth of substitution. The New Testament declares that the blood of goats could never take away sins, but Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12; 10:4). The brothers used blood to conceal guilt; God provides blood that cleanses it.

wordNotes.term: שְׂעִיר עִזִּים (se‘ir ‘izzim) — a kid of the goats
wordNotes.explanation: Se‘ir means “hairy one,” a male goat, and ‘izzim specifies goats. The term is used frequently for the goat of the sin offering (Leviticus 4:23; 16:9). The word se‘ir also recalls Esau, the hairy man who lived in Seir (Genesis 27:11; 36:8), adding another echo of Jacob’s deception of Isaac. Judah will later promise Tamar “a kid from the flock” (Genesis 38:17).

verses.bibleText: And they sent the coat of many colours, and they brought it to their father; and said, This have we found: know now whether it be thy son's coat or no.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they sent the coat of many colours, and they brought it to their father.” The Hebrew suggests that the brothers sent the robe ahead by messenger, perhaps a servant, and then came themselves. They avoid being present when Jacob first sees it, sparing themselves his initial grief and the risk of betraying their guilt.

Their message is carefully worded: “This have we found: know now whether it be thy son’s coat or no.” They do not lie outright. They say they found the robe, which in a sense is true, and they invite Jacob to draw his own conclusion. They call Joseph “thy son,” not “our brother,” distancing themselves from him even in speech.

The phrase “know now” is the same expression Tamar will use with Judah in the next chapter when she produces his seal, cord, and staff: “Discern, I pray thee, whose are these” (38:25). There Judah is forced to recognise his own guilt and confess, “She hath been more righteous than I” (38:26). The repetition shows that God holds Judah, the architect of Joseph’s sale, accountable through a similar act of recognition. Truth hidden by deception will eventually come to light (Numbers 32:23; Luke 12:2).

wordNotes.term: הַכֶּר־נָא (hakker-na) — know now
wordNotes.explanation: The Hiphil imperative of nakar, “to recognise, identify,” with the particle na. The verb links several moments of deception in Genesis. Isaac “discerned him not” when Jacob came in disguise (Genesis 27:23), Judah is asked to recognise his pledge (Genesis 38:25), and Joseph “knew his brethren, but they knew not him” (Genesis 42:8). The brothers invite Jacob to recognise the robe and draw the wrong conclusion.

verses.bibleText: And he knew it, and said, It is my son's coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he knew it, and said, It is my son’s coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.” Jacob recognises the robe at once. He reaches the conclusion his sons intended, repeating their very words, “an evil beast hath devoured him” (v. 20). The deception works perfectly. Jacob never suspects his sons.

His words come in three short cries, each more desperate than the last. First, recognition: “It is my son’s coat.” Then explanation: a wild animal has killed him. Finally, the image that fills his mind: “Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.” The Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis, “torn, torn is Joseph.” The bloodied robe, perhaps also torn, offered no hope that the boy had escaped.

The robe that symbolised Jacob’s favouritism has become the sign of his loss. The truth is more terrible than he knows, for his son was “torn” from him by the jealousy of his brothers rather than the claws of a beast. Yet the truth is also more hopeful, because Joseph is alive. Jacob will repeat his conclusion years later, saying of Joseph, “Surely he is torn in pieces; and I saw him not since” (44:28). Not until his sons return from Egypt with the news that Joseph is alive will his spirit revive (45:26-28).

wordNotes.term: טָרֹף טֹרַף יוֹסֵף (taroph toraf yosef) — Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces
wordNotes.explanation: Taraf means “to tear, rend,” used of wild animals tearing prey. The infinitive with the finite verb intensifies the statement: “surely torn.” The law dealt with animals “torn of beasts” (Exodus 22:13, 31), and Jacob reminded Laban that he had borne the loss of what was torn by beasts (Genesis 31:39). Jacob repeats the phrase in Genesis 44:28.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days.” Jacob performs every customary act of mourning. He tears his garments as Reuben had done (v. 29), puts on sackcloth, and mourns for an extended period. This is the first mention of sackcloth in Scripture. It was coarse cloth woven from goat or camel hair, the same material used for sacks of grain (42:25), and worn as a sign of grief, humiliation, or repentance (2 Samuel 3:31; Jonah 3:5-8).
