His mourning is described as lasting “many days.” Customary mourning periods in Israel and Egypt were measured, seven days or thirty days or, in Egypt, seventy days (50:3, 10; Deuteronomy 34:8). Jacob’s grief knows no such limit. He could not bury Joseph, for there was no body, and the absence of a grave made closure impossible.

The scene also shows the long reach of hidden sin. The brothers’ crime did not end at Dothan; it lived on in their father’s house every day he wore sackcloth. Each time they saw him mourning, they were reminded of what they had done, and their silence became a burden of its own. Twenty years later, under pressure in Egypt, their first instinct was to connect their trouble with Joseph (42:21). Concealed sin does not stay buried; it weighs on the conscience until it is confessed (Psalm 32:3-5).

Jacob’s sorrow is moving. The man who had once deceived his father and fled his brother now suffers through his own children’s deception. Yet his grief is real and his love for Joseph sincere. Scripture does not mock human sorrow. Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus (John 11:35), and Paul tells believers they grieve, but not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Jacob’s grief, as the next verse shows, was the sorrow of a man who thought his hope had died.

wordNotes.term: שַׂק (saq) — sackcloth
wordNotes.explanation: Saq is a coarse fabric, usually of goat hair, and also the word for a grain sack (Genesis 42:25, 35). Worn on the loins, it was a sign of mourning and humiliation (1 Kings 21:27; Esther 4:1). Jesus spoke of cities that would have repented “in sackcloth and ashes” had they seen his works (Matthew 11:21).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתְאַבֵּל (vayyit’abbel) — and mourned
wordNotes.explanation: The Hithpael of ’aval, “to mourn,” describes engaging in the rites and behaviour of mourning. Samuel mourned for Saul (1 Samuel 15:35), and David mourned for Absalom many days (2 Samuel 13:37). The verb speaks of visible, sustained grief rather than a passing feeling.

verses.bibleText: And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted.” The whole family gathers around Jacob. The mention of “all his daughters” likely includes his daughters-in-law as well as Dinah, since Hebrew often uses family terms broadly, though Genesis 46:7 suggests he may have had more daughters. The scene is bitter with irony. The brothers who sold Joseph now try to console the father whose heart they have broken. Their comfort cannot reach him, for it is based on a lie, and the only words that could help, “Joseph is alive,” they will not speak.

Jacob “refused to be comforted.” Jeremiah used the same words of Rachel weeping for her children in Ramah (Jeremiah 31:15), and Matthew applied that verse to the mothers of Bethlehem when Herod killed their sons (Matthew 2:18). In each case grief seems beyond consolation, and in each case God’s purpose was still moving forward. Joseph lived, and the child Jesus was preserved in Egypt.

“For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning.” The word for grave is she’ol, appearing here for the first time in Scripture. Jacob means that he will mourn until his own death, when he will join Joseph in the realm of the dead. Since Jacob believed Joseph’s body had been devoured, he could not be thinking of a literal family tomb. Sheol is the common grave of humanity, the state of all who have died, whether righteous or wicked (Psalm 89:48; Ecclesiastes 9:10).

Scripture never describes sheol as a place where conscious souls dwell, rewarded or tormented. It is the place of silence where the dead do not praise God (Psalm 6:5; 115:17) and “know not any thing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5). Jacob does not expect to meet Joseph’s living spirit; he expects to share Joseph’s death. The Old Testament hope for the dead lies not in an immortal soul but in God’s power to raise them. “I will ransom them from the power of the grave,” God promises (Hosea 13:14), and Paul quotes this when he describes the resurrection at Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:54-55). Job likewise looked to that day when he asked God to hide him in sheol until his wrath was past and then to call him (Job 14:13-15).

“Thus his father wept for him.” The closing words underline the depth of Jacob’s sorrow. He would weep for Joseph for more than twenty years, never knowing that his son was alive and that God was preparing a reunion beyond his hopes (46:29-30).

wordNotes.term: שְׁאֹלָה (she’olah) — into the grave
wordNotes.explanation: She’ol with a directional ending, “to Sheol.” This is the word’s first occurrence. It denotes the grave or the realm of the dead, the common destination of all humanity (Psalm 89:48). Scripture describes it as a place of silence and darkness where there is no work, knowledge, or praise (Ecclesiastes 9:10; Psalm 6:5). It is not a place of conscious souls; the dead rest there until God raises them (Psalm 49:15; Hosea 13:14). The Greek Old Testament renders it hades, the term used in Acts 2:27, 31 of Christ’s body not abandoned to the grave.

wordNotes.term: וַיְמָאֵן לְהִתְנַחֵם (vayma’en lehitnachem) — he refused to be comforted
wordNotes.explanation: Ma’en means “to refuse,” and the Hithpael of nacham means “to be comforted, console oneself.” The phrase is used again of Rachel weeping for her children (Jeremiah 31:15) and of a soul in distress (Psalm 77:2). Isaiah promises that the Lord himself will comfort his people (Isaiah 40:1; 51:12).

verses.bibleText: And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, and captain of the guard.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard.” The chapter closes with a sudden shift of scene. While Jacob weeps in Hebron believing his son is dead, Joseph is alive in Egypt, sold as a slave into the household of a high official. The juxtaposition is deliberate. Jacob’s grief is real, but his conclusion is false.

The name Potiphar is a shortened form of an Egyptian name meaning “he whom Ra has given,” similar to the name of Joseph’s future father-in-law, Potipherah (41:45). He is called a saris, a term that could mean “eunuch” but was also used more generally of court officials. He held the office of “captain of the guard,” literally “chief of the slaughterers,” probably commander of the royal bodyguard or executioners. Joseph has been sold into a prominent household near the centre of Egyptian power.

This verse prepares for the story to resume in chapter 39, after the account of Judah and Tamar. In Potiphar’s house Joseph will rise to oversee all his master’s affairs, then be falsely accused and thrown into prison, where he will meet the officials of Pharaoh whose dreams lead to his exaltation. God had told Abraham that his descendants would sojourn in a land not theirs (15:13), and through Joseph’s sale that word begins to be fulfilled.

The chapter ends on a note of hidden hope. God is not mentioned once in Genesis 37, yet his providence runs through every scene. Joseph would later say to his brothers, “Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive” (50:20). Paul’s words to believers in every generation rest on the same truth: “All things work together for good to them that love God” (Romans 8:28).

wordNotes.term: סְרִיס פַּרְעֹה (seris par‘oh) — an officer of Pharaoh’s
wordNotes.explanation: Saris can mean “eunuch” (Isaiah 56:3-4), but it is also used of royal officials generally. Potiphar was married (Genesis 39:7), and the term is applied to Pharaoh’s butler and baker (Genesis 40:2). In the New Testament the Ethiopian official baptized by Philip is called a eunuch and a man of great authority (Acts 8:27).

wordNotes.term: שַׂר הַטַּבָּחִים (sar hattabbachim) — captain of the guard
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “chief of the slaughterers.” Tabbach can mean a cook or butcher (1 Samuel 9:23), but in royal contexts it denotes a bodyguard or executioner. The same title is used of Nebuzaradan, Nebuchadnezzar’s commander who destroyed Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:8), and Arioch, Nebuchadnezzar’s officer in Daniel (Daniel 2:14).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When jealousy takes root in a family or a church, where does it usually lead if no one confronts it?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Favouritism, pride, and envy drive Joseph’s family to betray him, yet God is already steering the evil deeds of the brothers toward the saving of many lives, as he would later do through the rejection of his own Son.
discussionQuestions: How did Jacob’s own history make his favouritism toward Joseph especially unwise?
What steps can you trace in the brothers’ hearts from resentment to hatred to the plan to kill?
Why do you think Jacob rebuked Joseph yet still “observed the saying”?
Where do you see God’s providence in the chapter even though he is never named?
In what ways does Joseph’s rejection by his brothers anticipate the rejection of Jesus, and where should the comparison stop?
commonMisunderstandings: The chapter does not present Joseph as flawless; his tale-bearing and his eagerness to recount his dreams added fuel to the fire, even though the brothers alone bear the guilt of their crime.

Jacob’s words about going down “into the grave” (sheol) do not describe a realm where Joseph’s conscious soul awaited him; sheol is the grave, the state of death, where the dead rest until the resurrection.
The shift between “Ishmeelites” and “Midianites” does not reveal two contradictory stories; the names describe the same caravan of traders (compare Judges 8:22-24).
God’s use of the brothers’ evil does not excuse it; Scripture holds them accountable while showing that he overruled their intent for good (Genesis 50:20).
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the human drama and the divine purpose together: trace honestly how sin grows in a family, then show how God works through rejection to raise up a deliverer, a pattern fulfilled in Christ (Acts 7:9-10).
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring your jealousies and family wounds to the God who saw Joseph in the pit, and trust the Saviour who was rejected by his own to bring you through your darkest road.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s providence overrules human sin to accomplish salvation, foreshadowed in Joseph and fulfilled in Christ, who was rejected by his brethren and sold, yet exalted to save.
flow: Joseph’s family shows the destructive power of favouritism, envy, and hatred left unchecked.
The brothers try to destroy God’s revealed purpose by getting rid of the dreamer.
God never leaves Joseph; every step toward Egypt becomes a step toward his exaltation.
Jesus likewise came to his own, was rejected, sold for silver, and handed over to death, yet God raised and exalted him as Saviour.
The same God invites us to repent of envy and to trust him in our own pits and losses.
simpleIllustrations: A weaver working on the back of a tapestry sees only knots and loose ends, while the pattern is visible from the front; Joseph saw the knots in the pit, but God saw the finished design.
A small spark of resentment left in dry grass can become a wildfire; the brothers’ envy began with a coat and a report and ended in a crime that grieved their father for twenty years.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let go of resentment toward others and trust the rejected and exalted Saviour to work his purpose in your life?
cautions: Do not allegorize every detail of Joseph’s story into a picture of Christ; keep the parallels the New Testament itself suggests.
Do not suggest that God caused the brothers to sin; he permitted and overruled their free choices.
Do not teach from verse 35 that the dead are conscious in sheol; Scripture presents death as a sleep until the resurrection.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to show favouritism, and what damage might it be doing to those around me?
Is there resentment in my heart toward someone God has blessed more visibly than me?
How do I handle the things God has shown me: with Jacob’s patient pondering or with Joseph’s eager telling?
When I feel thrown into a pit, do I believe God is still guiding my steps?
What does it mean to me that Jesus, like Joseph, was rejected by his own and yet exalted to save?
